title: Build & Dependency Management
summary: Build once, promote everywhere only works if the build is actually reproducible. Learn lockfiles, artifact repositories, pinned vs floating dependencies, and the supply-chain basics interviewers now expect.

slides.markdown:
"Build once, promote everywhere" (from Pipeline Design) only holds if a build actually produces the same output every time you run it. If your dependency resolution can silently pull a different version tomorrow than it did today, you don't have one artifact — you have an illusion of one.

This topic is about making that illusion real: reproducible builds, lockfiles that pin the entire dependency tree, artifact repositories as the source of truth, and the supply-chain basics — SBOMs, signed artifacts — that have moved from "nice to have" to something interviewers now expect you to know exists.

A build is **reproducible** if the same input — same source, same dependency versions, same build environment — produces the same output, byte for byte, every time. That sounds obvious, but plenty of real build systems violate it: a `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` with unpinned versions pulls whatever's newest *today*, a build timestamp gets baked into the binary, or a compiler flag depends on the host machine's default locale.

Reproducibility matters because it's the precondition for "build once, promote everywhere" meaning anything. If rebuilding from the exact same commit can produce a different artifact, then "this passed staging" no longer implies "this is what's in production" — you've silently reintroduced the per-environment-rebuild risk that build-once was supposed to eliminate.

A manifest like `package.json` or `pyproject.toml` declares your **direct** dependencies, often with a version *range* (`^4.2.0`). That range is exactly the ambiguity reproducibility can't tolerate — it doesn't say which exact version was actually installed, including all the **transitive** dependencies pulled in underneath.

A **lockfile** (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `Cargo.lock`) resolves that ambiguity once and records the exact version of every package in the tree, direct and transitive, plus often a content hash. Installing from the lockfile — not re-resolving the manifest — is what makes "install dependencies" produce the identical tree every time, on every machine, forever, until someone deliberately updates the lockfile.

slides.sectionTitle: Artifact repositories as the source of truth
slides.markdown:
Once a build produces an artifact — a container image, a `.jar`, a Python wheel — it gets pushed to an **artifact repository** (a container registry, Artifactory, Nexus, npm's own registry for your internal packages) under an immutable tag, usually the commit SHA or a semantic version.

This repository, not any particular build server or CI run, becomes the **source of truth** for what's actually deployable. "Deploy `myapp:a1b2c3`" means "pull this exact object from the registry" — nothing gets rebuilt, nothing gets re-resolved. If the registry is unavailable or the tag doesn't exist, that's a hard failure, not a fallback-to-rebuild — a rebuild at deploy time is exactly the non-reproducibility this whole practice exists to prevent.

| Strategy | Behavior | Risk | Update effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Floating** (`^4.2.0`, `latest`) | Auto-picks newest matching version at install time | High — behavior can change with no code change on your side | None — but that's the problem |
| **Fully pinned** (`4.2.1` exact, lockfile committed) | Always the same version until someone changes it | Low immediate risk, but security patches don't arrive automatically | Manual — someone has to bump it |
| **Pinned + scheduled updates** (Dependabot/Renovate PRs) | Pinned day to day, automated PRs propose bumps on a cadence | Low — updates are visible, reviewed, and tested via normal CI | Low-to-moderate — review the automated PRs |

Pinned-with-scheduled-updates is the practical sweet spot most mature teams land on: it gets the reproducibility of pinning with the security-patch cadence of floating, but every update goes through the same review and CI gate as any other code change, instead of silently happening at install time.

Two terms that moved from niche to expected knowledge after several high-profile supply-chain attacks (compromised packages shipping malware through trusted registries):

- **SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)** — a generated manifest listing every dependency, direct and transitive, in a shipped artifact, often with version and license info. When a vulnerability is disclosed in some library, an SBOM lets you grep for "do any of our shipped artifacts contain this" in seconds instead of manually auditing every service.
- **Signed artifacts** — a cryptographic signature over the built artifact, proving it came from your actual build pipeline and hasn't been tampered with in transit or at rest in the registry. Deployment tooling can verify the signature before running anything, rejecting an artifact that doesn't match.

Neither replaces the basics (lockfiles, pinning) — they add a layer of *verification* on top: not just "we know what's in this build" but "we can prove it, and prove it wasn't swapped."

slides.sectionTitle: A lockfile diff in a pull request
slides.markdown:
Most of the time a lockfile diff is noise you skim past — but a diff like this is worth stopping on:

```diff
- "left-pad": {
-   "version": "1.3.0",
-   "resolved": "https://registry.npmjs.org/left-pad/-/left-pad-1.3.0.tgz",
-   "integrity": "sha512-Xa..."
- },
+ "left-pad": {
+   "version": "1.3.0",
+   "resolved": "https://mirror.example.com/left-pad/-/left-pad-1.3.0.tgz",
+   "integrity": "sha512-Zb..."
+ },
```

Same version number, but the **resolved URL and integrity hash both changed** — meaning the bytes behind that version string are different from what was previously trusted, pulled from an unfamiliar mirror. That combination is a classic supply-chain red flag: a version bump should change the hash because it's genuinely different code; an *unchanged* version number with a *changed* hash means something was swapped underneath the same label.

Tools like Dependabot and Renovate open an automated PR every time a pinned dependency has a newer version available, running it through CI like any other change. This solves the "pinned dependencies never get security patches" problem — but it creates a new one: **review burden**. A team with hundreds of dependencies can face dozens of these PRs a week, and reviewing each one properly (reading changelogs, checking for breaking changes) doesn't scale to that volume.

Teams that manage this well triage rather than review everything equally: auto-merge patch-level bumps that pass CI with no human review, require human review for minor/major bumps, and prioritize security-flagged updates above routine ones — rather than either ignoring the PRs (which defeats the purpose) or reviewing all of them with equal, unsustainable rigor.

slides.sectionTitle: An unpinned dependency changing behavior silently
slides.markdown:
A service's `requirements.txt` specifies `requests>=2.20`. It's been stable for two years. One Tuesday, a routine redeploy — no code changes — starts failing intermittently. The cause: a new `requests` release, satisfying `>=2.20` and pulled automatically at install time, changed a default timeout behavior in a way that interacts badly with a slow downstream dependency.

The debugging cost here is disproportionate to the actual change: nobody touched the application code, so the natural instinct is to suspect infrastructure or the downstream service, not a dependency that "didn't change." The only reason it's findable at all is comparing the lockfile (if one exists) between the last-known-good deploy and the failing one — which is exactly the artifact a floating, unpinned dependency doesn't give you.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this fits with the rest of CI/CD
slides.markdown:
Everything here is in service of one property: **the artifact that passed your tests is provably the artifact running in production, and you can regenerate it exactly if you ever need to.** Pipeline Design's build-once-promote-everywhere assumes this is true; this topic is what actually makes it true.

The hierarchy, roughly: pin dependencies (lockfiles) so the build is deterministic; push the result to a registry (artifact repository) as the single source of truth; layer provenance on top (SBOMs, signing) so you can prove and audit what's in it; and manage the update cadence (Dependabot-style automation with triage) so pinning doesn't mean permanently stale.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: pinning is not the whole answer
slides.markdown:
A common junior mistake is treating "pin everything and never update" as the safe answer. It isn't — a fully pinned dependency tree that's never updated accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities silently, and eventually a security audit or a breach forces a painful, all-at-once mass upgrade across years of drift at once.

The senior framing is a **cadence**, not a one-time lock: pin for determinism, automate update proposals for currency, and triage them so review effort scales with actual risk (security-flagged and major bumps get real scrutiny; routine patch bumps that pass CI can often auto-merge). Reproducibility and staying current aren't in tension — they're two properties you get by combining pinning with disciplined, automated review, not by picking one and ignoring the other.
